title: Charge, Current, Resistance & Power
description: Electrostatics and the electron model, current and charge, e.m.f. versus potential difference, resistance and its measurement, I–V characteristics, electrical power, energy and the kilowatt-hour for IGCSE Physics 0625.

notes.heading: Charge, Electrostatics and the Electron Model
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Electric **charge** is a property of matter measured in **coulombs (C)**. There are two types — positive and negative: like charges repel, unlike charges attract. An object becomes charged by gaining or losing **electrons**.

🔑 How it works
Rubbing a polythene rod with a cloth transfers electrons from the cloth onto the rod: the rod becomes negative and the cloth is left equally positive. Only electrons ever move in a solid — the positive nuclei stay fixed in place, so an object that LOSES electrons becomes positive. A charged object can also attract a neutral one by inducing a charge separation in it (why a rubbed balloon sticks to a wall). Earthing — connecting an object to the ground — lets excess charge flow away safely.

Conductors (metals, graphite) contain **free (delocalised) electrons** that can drift through the material. Insulators (plastic, glass, rubber, dry air) have no free electrons, so charge stays where it is put.

Supplement: an **electric field** is a region where an electric charge experiences a force. Field lines point in the direction of the force on a positive charge (from + towards −). Around a point charge the pattern is radial; between oppositely charged parallel plates the lines are straight, parallel and evenly spaced — a uniform field.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing 'positive charge flows onto the rod'. In solids only electrons move; the exam mark is for naming electrons and stating their direction of transfer.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Charge is measured in coulombs; like charges repel, unlike attract.
• Friction transfers electrons only; charge is conserved, never created.
• Conductors have free electrons; insulators do not.

✅ Check
A glass rod rubbed with silk becomes positive. Which way did the electrons move? (From the rod onto the silk — the rod lost electrons.)

notes.heading: Electric Current: I = Q/t, d.c. and a.c.
notes.body:
📌 Definition
An **electric current** is the rate of flow of charge (the Core definition — learn it word for word). Current is measured in **amperes (A)** with an ammeter connected in series. Supplement: the defining equation is

$$I = \dfrac{Q}{t}$$

where $Q$ is the charge in coulombs and $t$ the time in seconds, so $1\text{ A} = 1\text{ C/s}$.

🔑 How it works
In a metal wire the current is a drift of free electrons from the negative terminal towards the positive. **Conventional current** is defined the other way — from positive to negative — and this is the direction used in circuit rules and on circuit diagrams. **Direct current (d.c.)** flows in one direction only (cells, batteries). **Alternating current (a.c.)** repeatedly reverses direction (mains supply).

💡 Worked Example
A charge of 90 C passes a point in a wire in 30 s: $I = \dfrac{Q}{t} = \dfrac{90}{30} = 3\text{ A}$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Leaving the time in minutes. The $t$ in $I = \dfrac{Q}{t}$ must be in seconds — convert before dividing.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Current = charge per unit time; the unit is the ampere.
• Electron flow is − to +; conventional current is + to −.
• d.c. flows one way; a.c. reverses repeatedly.

✅ Check
Rearranged, $Q = It$: a 2 A current for 10 s delivers 20 C.

notes.heading: e.m.f. and Potential Difference
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The **electromotive force (e.m.f.)** of a source is the electrical energy supplied per unit charge in driving charge round the complete circuit. The **potential difference (p.d.)** between two points is the energy transferred per unit charge between those two points. Both are measured in volts, and $1\text{ V} = 1\text{ J/C}$. Supplement equations: e.m.f. $E = \dfrac{W}{Q}$ and p.d. $V = \dfrac{W}{Q}$, where $W$ is the energy in joules and $Q$ the charge in coulombs.

🔑 How it works
The e.m.f. belongs to the SOURCE (cell, battery, generator) — it is the 'push' given to each coulomb. A p.d. belongs to a COMPONENT — it is the energy converted per coulomb as charge passes through it. Measure a p.d. with a voltmeter connected **in parallel** across the component; measure the e.m.f. with a voltmeter across the source terminals.

💡 Worked Example
A 6 V battery supplies 6 J of energy to every coulomb it drives round the circuit. If the p.d. across a lamp is 6 V, that lamp converts 6 J of electrical energy for every coulomb that passes through it.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing 'energy per second' — that is power, not voltage. Both exam definitions say **per unit charge**. And e.m.f. is not a force in newtons: it is measured in volts.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• e.m.f. = energy supplied per coulomb by the source; p.d. = energy transferred per coulomb between two points.
• In a simple circuit the p.d.s across the components add up to the e.m.f.

✅ Check
A battery transfers 300 J while driving 50 C round a circuit: its e.m.f. is $\dfrac{300}{50} = 6\text{ V}$.

notes.heading: Resistance and the Voltmeter–Ammeter Practical
notes.body:
📌 Definition
**Resistance** is the opposition to the flow of current, defined by

$$R = \dfrac{V}{I}$$

and measured in **ohms (Ω)**. A component has a resistance of $1\ \Omega$ if a p.d. of 1 V drives a current of 1 A through it.

🔑 How it works — the Core practical
To measure the resistance of a wire or component: connect it with an **ammeter in series** and a **voltmeter in parallel** across it, and include a variable resistor (rheostat) so the current can be changed without rebuilding the circuit. Record several pairs of V and I values, then calculate $R = \dfrac{V}{I}$ for each pair (or take the gradient of a V–I graph).

💡 Worked Example
The voltmeter reads 6.0 V and the ammeter 0.5 A: $R = \dfrac{6.0}{0.5} = 12\ \Omega$.

What changes a wire's resistance (qualitative, Core): a **longer** wire has more resistance; a **thinner** wire has more resistance; the **material** matters (nichrome has far more resistance than the same size of copper); and a metal wire's resistance **rises as it gets hotter**.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Inverting the ratio: $R = \dfrac{V}{I}$, never $\dfrac{I}{V}$. Sanity-check the answer: 12 Ω at 6 V should return the 0.5 A you started with.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $R = \dfrac{V}{I}$; ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel, rheostat to vary the current.
• Longer, thinner or hotter metal wires resist more.

✅ Check
Doubling the p.d. across a fixed resistor doubles the current — the ratio $R$ stays constant.

notes.heading: Resistance Rules and I–V Characteristics (Supplement)
notes.body:
Supplement — quantifying resistance and reading I–V graphs.

🔑 Length and area
For a wire of a given material, $R \propto L$ (double the length, double the resistance) and $R \propto \dfrac{1}{A}$ (double the cross-sectional area, halve the resistance). Both changes together multiply: a wire twice as long with half the area has FOUR times the resistance.

🔑 I–V characteristics
Plot current against p.d. for each component:
• **Fixed resistor** — a straight line through the origin: the resistance is constant (an **ohmic conductor**).
• **Filament lamp** — a curve that gets flatter as V rises: the filament heats up, its resistance increases, so the current rises less and less steeply.
• **Diode** — conducts strongly in the forward direction once a small threshold voltage is passed, but carries almost no current in reverse: a one-way valve for current.

💡 Worked Example
Wire A has resistance 4 Ω. Wire B is the same material and thickness but three times as long: $R_B = 3 \times 4 = 12\ \Omega$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Reading the filament lamp's flattening curve as 'resistance decreasing'. A flatter I–V line means LESS current per volt — the resistance has INCREASED.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $R \propto L$ and $R \propto \dfrac{1}{A}$.
• Straight line = ohmic resistor; flattening curve = filament lamp; one-way = diode.

✅ Check
Which has the greater resistance: 2 m of a nichrome wire, or 1 m of the identical wire? (The 2 m length — exactly double.)

illustration.alt: Three I–V characteristic graphs: a straight line through the origin for a fixed resistor, a flattening curve for a filament lamp, and a one-way curve for a diode.
illustration.caption: The shape of an I–V graph identifies the component: straight line = constant resistance, flattening curve = filament lamp heating up, one-way = diode.

notes.heading: Electrical Power and Energy: P = IV and E = IVt
notes.body:
📌 Definition
**Electrical power** is the rate at which energy is transferred:

$$P = IV$$

measured in **watts (W)**, where $1\text{ W} = 1\text{ J/s}$. The energy transferred in time $t$ is

$$E = IVt$$

in joules, with $t$ in seconds.

🔑 How it works
A component with a p.d. $V$ across it and a current $I$ through it converts $IV$ joules every second. This is why appliance ratings tell you their power: a '230 V, 10 A' shower is a $P = 230 \times 10 = 2300\text{ W}$ device.

💡 Worked Example
A 12 V lamp draws 0.5 A for 100 s: $E = IVt = 0.5 \times 12 \times 100 = 600\text{ J}$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using $P = \dfrac{V}{I}$, or forgetting to convert minutes to seconds in $E = IVt$ — 5 minutes is 300 s, not 5 s.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $P = IV$ in watts; $E = IVt$ in joules with $t$ in seconds.
• Power is energy transferred per second.

✅ Check
A 230 V, 2 A kettle element: $P = 2 \times 230 = 460\text{ W}$, transferring 460 J every second.

notes.heading: The Kilowatt-hour and Electricity Bills
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The **kilowatt-hour (kWh)** is the energy transferred by a 1 kW appliance running for 1 hour:

$$1\text{ kWh} = 1000\text{ W} \times 3600\text{ s} = 3.6 \times 10^{6}\text{ J}$$

Electricity companies bill per kWh — the 'unit' on a bill. Cost = energy used in kWh × price per kWh.

🔑 How it works
Convert the power to kilowatts, multiply by the hours of use, then by the price per kWh. High-power appliances (heaters, kettles, ovens) dominate a bill because it is power, not just time, that multiplies the cost.

💡 Worked Example
A 2 kW heater runs for 3 hours with electricity at 30 p per kWh: energy $= 2 \times 3 = 6\text{ kWh}$, cost $= 6 \times 30\text{ p} = 180\text{ p} =$ £$1.80$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting to convert watts to kilowatts: a 500 W appliance is 0.5 kW, not 500 kW. Household answers should come out in pennies or a few pounds — thousands of pounds means the kilowatt step was skipped.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The kWh is an ENERGY unit: power in kW × time in h.
• Cost = kWh used × price per kWh.

✅ Check
A 100 W lamp (0.1 kW) left on for 10 h uses exactly 1 kWh — one 'unit' of electricity.

flashcards.definition: A property of matter measured in coulombs (C). Two types: like charges repel, unlike charges attract.
flashcards.example: A rubbed balloon carries a static charge and attracts small pieces of paper.

flashcards.definition: Rubbing transfers ELECTRONS between two insulators. The one gaining electrons becomes negative; the other is left equally positive.
flashcards.example: Polythene rubbed with cloth gains electrons → negative rod, positive cloth.

flashcards.definition: A material containing free (delocalised) electrons that can move through it, so charge flows.
flashcards.example: Copper, all metals and graphite conduct; wiring uses copper.

flashcards.definition: A material with no free electrons, so charge cannot flow through it and stays where it is put.
flashcards.example: Plastic, glass, rubber and dry air insulate — cable coatings are plastic.

flashcards.definition: The rate of flow of charge: $I = \dfrac{Q}{t}$, measured in amperes (A). $1\text{ A} = 1\text{ C/s}$.
flashcards.example: 90 C passing in 30 s gives $I = \dfrac{90}{30} = 3\text{ A}$.

flashcards.definition: Direct current flows in one direction only (cells, batteries); alternating current repeatedly reverses direction (mains supply).
flashcards.example: A torch runs on d.c. from cells; a desk lamp runs on a.c. from the mains.

flashcards.definition: The electrical energy supplied per unit charge by a source in driving charge round the complete circuit. Measured in volts.
flashcards.example: A 6 V battery gives each coulomb 6 J of energy — e.m.f. $E = \dfrac{W}{Q}$.

flashcards.definition: The energy transferred per unit charge between two points in a circuit. $1\text{ V} = 1\text{ J/C}$; measured with a voltmeter in parallel.
flashcards.example: A lamp with 6 V across it converts 6 J for every coulomb that passes.

flashcards.definition: Opposition to current: $R = \dfrac{V}{I}$, measured in ohms (Ω). Longer, thinner, hotter metal wires have more resistance.
flashcards.example: 6.0 V across a component with 0.5 A through it: $R = 12\ \Omega$.

flashcards.definition: Fixed resistor: straight line through the origin (constant R). Filament lamp: curve flattens (R rises as it heats). Diode: conducts in one direction only.
flashcards.example: A straight I–V line through the origin identifies an ohmic conductor.

flashcards.definition: $P = IV$ in watts ($1\text{ W} = 1\text{ J/s}$); energy transferred $E = IVt$ in joules, with $t$ in seconds.
flashcards.example: 230 V and 2 A give $P = 460\text{ W}$ — 460 J converted every second.

flashcards.definition: The energy used by a 1 kW appliance in 1 hour: $3.6 \times 10^{6}\text{ J}$. Bills charge per kWh: cost = kW × hours × price.
flashcards.example: 2 kW for 3 h = 6 kWh; at 30 p per kWh the cost is £$1.80$.

questions.stem: Which particles move through a metal wire to carry the electric current?
questions.explanation: In a solid metal only electrons are free to move — the positive ions are locked in the lattice and protons and neutrons sit in the nuclei. A current in a wire is a drift of free electrons from the negative terminal towards the positive.

questions.stem: A polythene rod is rubbed with a dry cloth and becomes negatively charged. Which statement explains this?
choices: Electrons are transferred from the cloth onto the rod
Protons are transferred from the rod onto the cloth
Electrons are transferred from the rod onto the cloth
The friction creates new negative charge
questions.explanation: Charging by friction moves electrons only. Electrons transferred onto the rod leave it with more electrons than protons, so it is negative; the cloth is left equally positive. Charge is conserved — it is transferred, never created.

questions.stem: What is the unit of electric charge?
questions.explanation: Charge is measured in coulombs. The ampere is the unit of current (1 A = 1 C/s), the volt is energy per coulomb, and the ohm is the unit of resistance.

questions.stem: A steady current of 2 A flows through a lamp for 30 s. How much charge passes through the lamp?
questions.explanation: Rearranging $I = \dfrac{Q}{t}$: $Q = It = 2 \times 30 = 60\text{ C}$. The 15 C trap divides $t$ by $I$; 0.067 C is $\dfrac{I}{t}$.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares direct current (d.c.) and alternating current (a.c.)?
choices: d.c. repeatedly reverses direction; a.c. flows in one direction only
d.c. flows in one direction only; a.c. repeatedly reverses direction
d.c. is always a larger current than a.c.
a.c. can only be produced by a battery
questions.explanation: A cell or battery supplies d.c. — charge flows one way round the circuit. The mains supply is a.c. — the current reverses direction many times per second (50 times per second at 50 Hz).

questions.stem: What is meant by the electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a battery?
choices: The force the battery exerts on each electron, measured in newtons
The energy transferred per unit charge across a component in the circuit
The electrical energy supplied per unit charge in driving charge round the complete circuit
The maximum current the battery can supply
questions.explanation: The e.m.f. is a property of the SOURCE: the energy it supplies per coulomb to drive charge round the whole circuit, measured in volts. 'Energy transferred per unit charge across a component' is the potential difference — keeping the two definitions apart is what the exam marks.

questions.stem: A student must measure the current through a resistor and the potential difference across it. How should the two meters be connected?
choices: Ammeter in series with the resistor; voltmeter in parallel across it
Ammeter in parallel across the resistor; voltmeter in series with it
Both meters in series with the resistor
Both meters in parallel across the resistor
questions.explanation: An ammeter measures the charge flowing through a point each second, so it sits in series in the same loop. A voltmeter compares the energy per coulomb at two points, so it connects in parallel across the component.

questions.stem: A battery drives 60 C of charge round a circuit, transferring 240 J of chemical energy in doing so. What is the e.m.f. of the battery?
questions.explanation: e.m.f. $E = \dfrac{W}{Q} = \dfrac{240}{60} = 4\text{ V}$ — four joules supplied per coulomb. The 0.25 V trap divides $Q$ by $W$; 14400 V multiplies them.

questions.stem: In a resistance experiment the voltmeter across a fixed resistor reads 6.0 V when the ammeter reads 0.5 A. What is the resistance?
questions.explanation: $R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{6.0}{0.5} = 12\ \Omega$. The 3.0 Ω trap multiplies $V$ by $I$; 0.083 Ω inverts the ratio. Check: 12 Ω at 6 V gives 0.5 A — the original readings.

questions.stem: The I–V characteristic of a filament lamp is a curve that gets flatter as the voltage increases. Why does it have this shape?
choices: The filament obeys Ohm's law more closely as it heats up
The filament heats up as the current rises, so its resistance increases and the current rises less steeply
The lamp conducts in one direction only
The resistance falls because the filament gets hotter
questions.explanation: As the current grows, the filament gets hotter; the metal ions vibrate more and obstruct the drifting electrons, so the resistance rises. A higher resistance means less current per volt, so the I–V curve bends towards the voltage axis (flatter). The one-way description belongs to a diode.

questions.stem: A mains lamp operates at 230 V and draws a current of 2 A. What is its power?
questions.explanation: $P = IV = 2 \times 230 = 460\text{ W}$. The 115 W trap computes $\dfrac{V}{I}$ — that is the resistance formula $R$, not power.

questions.stem: Wire X has a resistance of 12 Ω. Wire Y is made of the same material but is twice as long and has half the cross-sectional area. What is the resistance of wire Y?
questions.explanation: Resistance is proportional to length (twice as long → ×2) and inversely proportional to area (half the area → ×2). The effects multiply: $R = 12 \times 2 \times 2 = 48\ \Omega$. The 24 Ω trap applies only the length change.

questions.stem: A current of 0.5 A flows through a component with 12 V across it for 2 minutes. How much energy is transferred?
questions.explanation: Convert 2 minutes to 120 s first: $E = IVt = 0.5 \times 12 \times 120 = 720\text{ J}$. The 12 J trap uses $t = 2$ instead of 120 s; 6 J is just the power $IV$ in watts.

questions.stem: A 2 kW heater is used for 3 hours. Electricity costs 30 p per kWh. What is the total cost?
questions.explanation: Energy used $= 2\text{ kW} \times 3\text{ h} = 6\text{ kWh}$. Cost $= 6 \times 30\text{ p} = 180\text{ p} =$ £$1.80$. The 60 p trap multiplies power by price without the time.

questions.stem: Two oppositely charged parallel metal plates produce an electric field between them. What does the field pattern look like?
choices: Radial lines spreading outwards from each plate
Lines running from the negative plate to the positive plate
Closed loops circulating between the plates
Straight, parallel, evenly spaced lines directed from the positive plate to the negative plate
questions.explanation: Between parallel plates the field is uniform: straight, parallel, evenly spaced lines. Field direction is defined as the direction of the force on a POSITIVE charge, so the lines run from the positive plate to the negative plate. Radial lines belong to a point charge, and electric field lines are never closed loops.
